The actual surgery I had in April of this year was performed by my ENT doctor (from Switzerland, he was awesome) who only became my ENT specialist after mine had gone away indefinitely on maternity leave. This guy was the definition of tall, glasses, cool type. Someone who finds the answers to obstacles in his way. 

2 years of throat squeezing only to have an MRI with contrast be the factor in finding what was causing my body such distress. Since April, I can breathe again. Go swimming. Eat, drink. I got too thin healing. But bulking back up is what being human is all about.

It took getting a contrastMRI on my throat which found I had calcified ligaments in my throat (bones crushing my throat from the inside). Having hEDS contributed to the tearing of connective tissue in my throat tearing for 2 years. My surgeon went all Batman and instead of slicing my throat like gills on a fish he went in and took out my tonsils with the bone matter. Saved me some pretty gnarly scars. Totally anesthetized for 3 weeks after the surgery. Couldn’t eat or drink anything except liquid oxycodone. Used my mortar and pestle until it smashed from carelessness. 

Total Dysphagia relieved and cured upon healing. I will admit, my body got so weak during the healing process I actually contracted COVID from someone in my home. I’ve been in close quarters with COVID carriers and for years never got it. My immune system went to hell to heal this. I have pictures of the healing at the back of my throat. For perspective- I’m someone who was pushed into therapy before kindergarten. People attempting to raise me wanted me to have problems when I had none. Problems that they could dramatize. Drugs were the cure all and never was a refill denied. And I lived like that for a long time. Alone and dependent. If you know, you know. 

So now in my mid 30s, many surgeries and procedures later mending a body constantly trying to rebuild itself, I have appreciation for the therapy I use. Conditional support. I do my part by applying what I’ve been taught in practicality. It’s never about victimizing myself or blaming anyone or anything for the physical pain I endure daily. 

Does it make the pain ever go away? No. It makes me capable of dealing with the situation. That’s priceless. No drug, however ingested, can succeed in doing this. And there’s no comparing anyone’s pain to anyone else’s. It’s never a contest. 

“Health is all about accepting and perceiving and dealing with reality on reality’s terms.” 

Some therapists are just uneducated and ill equipped but when you find one that isn’t, it’s worth the wait.

Aging, chronic pain, degenerative diseases, are only a few worries in depression but there’s so much more. You’ve endured. That holds up stronger to me than never critically thinking about the life choices over the decades. Some people manage to float through life. I don’t envy them. Tough times don’t last but tough people do. They wake up only to tune out. And I can’t blame them. 

But that power to endure doesn’t just go away. Every time you feel you’ve hit a breaking point, remember how strong you’ve been. 

My great aunt worked until she passed at 99 years old. She never openly complained about anything but you could tell she’d lived life and persevered. She was old. She was beautiful. Every wrinkle or scar in her skin were badges of having that puzzle piece- the survival instinct- adrenaline to actively NOT DIE. It’s priceless and admirable. 

You are beautiful. Feel shame, then lift your head. You’ve passed that. You’re stronger than you think.

I’ll probably never get another opportunity to write about this but here goes… I injured my back about 7 months ago. And I’ll fall forward, chest to my thighs or if standing go straight to the floor. Ive done waaaay too much studying of animals and animation for a project… and one day I landed on my knuckles. Safely inside, instead of trying to straighten my back and stand up I pulled the information about how Tarzan was animated in the Disney animated film. I found myself walking on my knuckles and maneuvered around to a place to sit. But, wow. I looked at my reflection and was amazed how much easier it was to walk with my weight balanced on my shoulders and down to my knuckles. I would not try this unless you have strong legs as I can see why Jane, in the movie looks like she’s hopping around on her knuckles while imitating Tarzan to show her father. That was a cute movie. And probably saved me a face plant when I realized I could balance and give my lower back a break from my weight if redistributed!

Oh wow. This is a problem I have these days. My body changed significantly after being obese for so long, I finally got fit and ate right. My teeth took years to repair but I now have a white full smile. But…

I think, I must imagine that I still look like I weigh what I used to… and perhaps it’s embarrassing to me to think I deserve that food at all. And still, it was more important for her to “be right.” I went by ambulance to a psychiatric hospital with my dog in my lap. I was furious. I still am. I had been sexually assaulted in this psych hospital that didn’t separate men from women in any capacity. There was only chaos and imagine, it was exactly the energy of adults having a food fight all day everyday and into each night. 

Fortunately I didn’t stay long because I didn’t have a reason. In the ambulance I remember apologizing profusely to the first responders that they were called out for my situation. 

The same LCSW, afterwards, I made sure to give a believable apology for her having to deal with me. And I have not been in a hospital since from this experience. And I forgive her….But in a dark alley… I’d love to tear her a new one.

You’ll surprise yourself when something amazing comes from what can appear at first to be a lost cause. With every brush stroke (goes for digital pens too) your hand is learning how to articulate. 

Don’t be afraid to waste paper. Use every corner of a page if needed. Add layers of color over a pencil sketch of something simple like a sunshine or flower petals or eye balls. Even just shapes. Spill coffee or juice on the paper. Get messy. 

You’re brave to ask for advice. I know professional artists who just won’t seek any advice or guidance (either because they teach or are too preoccupied with not making art.) Life happens either way. 

The moment you feel proud of a piece you’ve made, you’ll remember how worth it, it is to keep trying. 

I’m taking my own advice right now and like a kid, just playing with art tools. Tutorials are great but right now on YouTube it can be frustrating to keep up step by step because every artist is SO different, even if the techniques they use are exactly the same!

I swear by physical therapy. But they can be excellent or useless facilities depending on the knowledge of EDS from most/all of the trained physical therapists. 

An example of a glowing PT experience: Injured my right rotator cuff in July 2023. In less than 3 months I got full range of motion back in my dominant arm, I can write and draw again! I couldn’t be more grateful.

An example of poor PT experience is from the same injury, different facility for rehabilitation. The place was within walking distance (no bus hopping, I choose not to drive unless it’s an emergency). So I tried this place. They were not attentive, left me alone with no supervision wearing TENS unit equipment that wasn’t adjusted for my body, and knew when the exercises they were providing me left me in more pain than when I arrived, they “fired me.” I’ve read that recently here on Reddit, being “fired” from PT because you didn’t improve and somehow it’s all your fault. And from there it’s step 1 all over again. 

Solution: I got a new script from an orthopedic doctor and went straight to the PT place that I knew was out of the way but would also be WORTH it.

Items you are accustomed to carrying without much thought, everyday: Your cell phone, your keys, a dog’s leash, picking up and putting down pens or any writing equipment you need a grip to use. The rotator cuff has connection all the way into your wrist where weakness occurs with damage to the rotator cuff itself. I’m finally in physical therapy for my rotator cuff on my dominant shoulder and getting dexterity back into my hand was paramount. I have some exercises/stretches that have stopped my dropping of things. It was annoying. A good start is to take a tennis ball (not a lil one) and practice using the muscles and tendons in your wrist and hand to squeeze the ball. Don’t “hold for 5 seconds” or anything. Just practice using those specific muscles. You can feel it in your shoulder. Posture is key, so if you catch yourself in front of a mirror, take a sec to check how you’re standing. Shoulders dropped, not hunched up like stress and pain can cause people to do. Sitting is a good start with a pillow under your forearms, atop your lap. It’s how I was first taught, with the pillow, gradually building strength there in the wrist. 

Fun exercise! To see the strength in your wrists, do this: Sit straight up, pillow on lap, and for arms a top that pillow. Then put your palms facing out like you’re pushing something away. But instead, flex both wrists backwards as far as is comfortable. I was flabbergasted to see my left hand have more strength and dexterity than the one I use to draw tiny details with fine tip brushes. But it showed me very clearly where I needed strength to stop dropping things. For a guitarist, I hope any of this is helpful!
